newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-SOUTH AFRICAN SCANDAL NOT A SIGN OF RAMPANT RACISM.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-SOUTH AFRICAN SCANDAL NOT A SIGN OF RAMPANT RACISM.

text.p: South African rugby's latest visit to the public laundry to wash dirty linen from the apartheid era focused the spotlight once again on the extent to which racism still bedevils sport in Nelson Mandela's rainbow nation.
Springbok coach Andre Markgraaff's ugly tirade in which he described a top black rugby administrator as a "fucking kaffir" shows how little attitudes have changed among some.
But sports officials suggest his racist outburst was less the tip of the iceberg than the wagging tail of a departing dinosaur.

The fact that a tearful Markgraaff actually quit - and would have been sacked had he not - shows how far the sport has come. A few years ago the alleged "blackmailer" who taped his racist comments would have found no takers for his material.

But times are changing. Seventy thousand black soccer fans chant "Feeesh" every time white soccer player Mark Fish touches the ball for national side Bafana Bafana; coloured cricketer Paul Adams is mobbed by white kids for his autograph, and black Olympic marathon gold medallist Josia Thugwane is feted by all colours as a national hero.

Despite the Markgraaf scandal, Mvuzo Mbebe, chief executive of the National Sports Council, says sport is leading the way in racial reconciliation in South Africa. He also takes an historical perspective on the problem.

"Racism has been institutionalised in South African society for centuries and to expect that overnight it will go away would be asking a lot," he said. "There may be people who retain apartheid attitudes but by and large I believe there is no racism as such," he said.
"In fact, sports people have worked very hard to produce a transformation. In terms of racism and reconciliation sport is far more advanced than any other part of society in South Africa.
"Black soccer heroes are being perceived as heroes by white people and we are starting to see quite a lot of white people attending and participating in sports in townships," Mbebe added.

The United Cricket Board of South Africa (UCB) has budgeted over a million dollars to take cricket to the black townships this season. It has spent millions on the project since 1986 - long before Mandela's release was even contemplated.

"I like to think that the UCB are sincere and honest and have a vision to take cricket to all the people of South Africa," said Ali Bacher, managing director of the UCB, and a man in the vanguard of multi-racial sporting development.

Ironically, rugby union - perceived in many quarters as a game for white racists - is more popular than cricket among blacks, attracting 14 percent support to the nine percent of cricket in a recent poll.

Soccer is the most popular sport among blacks (77 percent) and also has a large white following, albeit rather different. While the man from Soweto will support Kaizer Chiefs or Orlando Pirates, his white neighbour in Johannesburg cheers for Manchester United.

Rugby's development programme for the new South Africa was slow to start but the game is trying to catch up. In 1996 it spent nearly four million dollars - two and a half times as much as cricket - on development.

Twenty more development officers were added to the existing 23, building work began on 42 township grounds, grants were made to 20 existing clubs in underprivileged areas, and 10 teenaged black and coloured players each spent a week with the Springboks in a programme called "rising stars".
Rian Oberholzer, chief executive of the South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) says: "Development is our number one priority. There is nothing more important to us.
"The perception that SARFU is not doing enough for rugby development is wrong. SARFU is rugby development."

Rugby has been played in Soweto since 1935 and cricket can only envy the number of black and particularly coloured players who have forced their way into Springbok teams on merit at all levels from 'A' team down.
History was made last season when coloured flanker Sean Plaatjies became the first non-white to captain the South African Schools' under-19 side.
However, rugby's programme is still sometimes seen as "T-shirt development" - take some T-shirts and media people into a township, hold a clinic and never go back again.
"There is that perception though I believe it is wrong," Mbebe said. "I believe they are trying their utmost in terms of development."
But development does not preclude racism. Markgraaff justifiably pointed to the steps Griqualand West had taken to bring black and coloured players into the provinces set up under his leadership.
But, under pressure, the dinosaur attitudes of the past were proved not yet extinct.
"There are a minority of racist people in sport. One needs to find ways of convincing them to embrace the new order. The first job is try and rehabilitate them," said Mbebe.
